query: Consider the following context: Phonon scattering by SRO precipitates might be expected to reduce scattering times and, therefore, decrease thermal conductivity. In that context, which material can be used for lattice heat conductivity, and why?

generation.intervention: Introduction of nanoprecipitates or modification of the alloy composition

falsification_experiment.design: Measure the lattice thermal conductivity of a high-entropy alloy with and without nanoprecipitates
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the introduction of nanoprecipitates does not lead to a reduction in lattice thermal conductivity, the hypothesis is falsified

cited_evidence.text: Paper card. Question: Can medium-entropy alloying be used to improve the thermoelectric performance of GeTe-based alloys?. System: GeTe-based alloys with compositions such as Ge0.63Mn0.15Pb0.1Sb0.06Cd0.06Te. Processing: Medium-entropy alloying by co-alloying Mn, Pb, Sb, and Cd with GeTe. Test conditions: Temperature range of 300-873 K. Findings: A state-of-the-art zT of 2.1 at 873 K; High average zT ave value of 1.3 between 300 and 873 K; Record high Vickers hardness of 270; Lattice thermal conductivity of 0.30 W m−1 K−1 at 873 K; Seebeck coefficient of 197 µV K−1 at 300 K and 248 µV K−1 at 773 K. Mechanism: The authors propose that medium-entropy alloying suppresses the phase transition, reduces lattice thermal conductivity, and enhances the Seebeck coefficient through band convergence and increased band effective mass. Limitations: The authors note that high-entropy alloying can lead to degraded carrier mobility, which needs to be compensated by band engineering. Future work: The authors suggest that further optimization of the alloy composition and microstructure could lead to even higher thermoelectric performance. Question: How do the phonon dynamics of the high-entropy alloy FeCoCrMnNi compare to those of glasses and complex metallic alloys (CMAs), and does it represent a unique class of materials?. System: Fe20Co20Cr20Mn20Ni20 (FeCoCrMnNi), a 5-element equiatomic FCC random solid solution.
